extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of philosophy/aesthetics interested in the nature of genius
extracted.subtask_description: A concise conceptual framework for recognising and distinguishing 'genius' and 'greatness' from mere talent or practical ability, based on psychological, moral, social, and somatic traits discussed in a philosophical essay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness = pursuit of objective ends (not personal concerns)
rubrics_metrics.description: He who seeks not his own concerns but pursues an objective end alone is 'great'; smallness is action directed to personal ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that greatness consists in working for the whole, not the individual; a true hero or genius lives for all. Even if the objective end is misunderstood or criminal, seeking the objective rather than personal gain makes one 'great'. Example/anti-pattern: actions motivated by transient personal interests are 'small'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius as intellect emancipated from service of the will
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is 'an intellect which has become untrue to its destination' — the intellect frees itself from serving the will and acts on its own account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This separation (intellect not bound to practical ends) is essential to genius and explains both its creative strengths and disadvantages; contrasted with the normal intellect, which remains in service of will and practical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: capacity for deeds vs capacity for works
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity for deeds (practical action) requires intellect in service of the will (decision, presence of mind); capacity for works (art, philosophy) demands objectivity and depth of knowledge from an intellect separated from the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men of deeds apply knowledge for practical ends; men of works require entire separation of intellect and thus are rarer. This criterion differentiates practical excellence from creative/theoretical greatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works of genius are essentially 'useless' (exist for their own sake)
rubrics_metrics.description: Productions of genius (music, philosophy, painting, poetry) serve no useful ends; to be of no use belongs to their character and is their 'patent of nobility'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrasts useful practical works (maintenance, easing existence) with artistic/intellectual creations which exist for their own sake. Examples: temples are not dwellings; garden-rose vs fruit-tree metaphor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius is often out of sync with its age and recognized late
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius 'comes into his age like a comet' and cannot go hand-in-hand with the regular progress of the culture; time must overtake genius's works, so recognition is generally late, often posthumous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why contemporaries often fail to appreciate genius; men of talent meet contemporary needs and are immediately prized, while genius transcends contemporaneous apprehension and is only trusted or accepted later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disadvantages of genius: impracticality, eccentricities, and risk of folly
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the genius's intellect is freed from the will, the individual may become useless in practical life and liable to eccentricities, personal slips, follies, and behaviours reminding of madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The intellect serving two 'masters' may leave the will inopportunely in a fix. Examples include being thrown into extreme emotions by trifles, inability to act suitably in urgent practical situations, and biographical evidence of unhappy life-courses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of soberness and hyper-sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius lacks 'soberness' — the power to see things only as they really are relative to ends — and exhibits hyper-sensibility (heightened nervous/cerebral system) combined with passionate vehemence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to exaggerated perceptions and extreme emotional reactions; associated with quick mood changes, melancholy, extravagance of disposition, and physical signs like strong cardiac pulsation. Example: Tasso's character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social isolation and poor fit for common conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius 'lives essentially alone' — too rare and different to be companionable; not adapted for thinking in common or ordinary conversation and thus has few friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their pleasures differ from the crowd's; they prefer the company of equals or the solitary production of works. Chamfort quote: excessive qualities can prevent many friendships. They are moral/personal beings but also belong to humanity as pure intellects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Childlike character: resemblance to childhood due to intellect predominance
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius shows a childlike character (naïveté, sublime simplicity) because, like children, their cerebral/nervous development predominates over other systems, producing more intellect than will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children are more disposed to theoretical occupation; genius retains this disproportion into adulthood. Examples: Mozart and Goethe described as 'big children'; claim that every child is to some extent a genius.

rubrics_metrics.name: Somatic/anatomical conditions favoring genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius is conditioned by anatomical and physiological qualities: abnormal predominance of sensibility over irritability and reproductive power; brain large (broad and high), fine/ excitable nerve-substance, favourable white-to-grey matter proportion, thin spinal cord/nerves, arched high skull, and overall good constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examples and data are cited (e.g., Byron's brain weight). The brain's configuration and proportion to other bodily systems are considered indispensable though not sufficient. A good stomach and energetic circulation (from the father) also matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological circulation/temperament contribution (paternal condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lively, passionate temperament (somatically energetic heart and circulation) contributed paternally is required alongside maternal brain qualities; it energizes the brain and contributes to genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why some inherit brain structure from mother and temperament from father; lack of the paternal circulatory condition yields talent without genius, while its presence without a well-constructed brain yields vivacity without mind (hot-headedness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex claim: women may have talent but not genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Assertion that 'women may have great talent, but no genius, for they always remain subjective.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a somatic/psychological claim in the essay; treated as a condition the author believes explains rarity of genius in women. (This is a historical philosophical claim and an explicit evaluative criterion in the text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward extremes when intellect focuses intensely
rubrics_metrics.description: When a genius concentrates all mental forces on an object, the rest of the world vanishes and the object fills all reality; this focus can magnify trivial things to monstrous proportions and throw the individual into violent emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This great concentration underlies great theoretical achievements but also causes exaggerated perception of everyday objects (flea becomes elephant under microscope analogy), producing extreme grief/joy/fear/anger from trifles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early development and later decline parallel: analogy with childhood and apes
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominance of the cerebral system in childhood (and in young apes) leads to early intellectual development that later declines as other systems (muscular, reproductive) predominate; genius retains the childhood-like intellectual predominance into adulthood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses comparative zoological and developmental evidence (orang-outang, Entelle) to argue that high early intelligence diminishing with age is natural, and genius is an abnormal persistence of that early predominance.
